title: Collapse-to-floor experiment: make runs finite (review R2)
description: Review finding 1 + rec 2, re-verified at HEAD: eval+notUp has unbounded loops — world full gives +6 forever alternating the two '+' tiles at (4,1)/(4,2); the +/x alternation ends only at move 42 because float ulp swallows the +6 and 'did not go UP' fires, not by design. Across 1500 generated seeds: 47.9% allow >=30 moves, 43.2% allow <=3, almost nothing between (0.4% in 10-29) — bimodal, no session-length runs. add+notUp unbounded in 92.7% of seeds; world d eval unbounded too. Proposal: after a collision the tile collapses to floor (re-entry = flat = fatal under notUp). Observation collapses superposition — the metaphor made literal; tile state stays position+superposition so it passes the primitives test in README 'Do not add'. Simulated at HEAD: >=30-move runs vanish (0.0%), 4-9 band grows 8.5% -> 47.5%, world full becomes a 5-move routing puzzle with best Number 243 — reproduces the review's simulation exactly. Caveats: (a) <=3 band grows to 52.4%, so first-move/onboarding work (sibling bead) matters MORE not less; (b) review's cheaper alternative — fatal step-back onto the cell just left — still leaves 1.0% of seeds unbounded (op-only 4-cycles never step back), so collapse is the structural fix; (c) implement as an opt-in experiment, not a global flip: registry flag or ?collapse=1 + a new variants.ts entry + variants/<id>.md notebook, and check per-variant interactions (Hoarder becomes a finite consume-everything puzzle — arguably truer to its hypothesis; Becoming gets forced forward motion). Red-green: engine/world tests + keep the headless distribution script to measure before/after. Playtest before making it the default for any existing variant.

title: Establish red-green TDD with a runner and a first real test
description:
Adopt red-green TDD for Number Up, independent of the TypeScript migration. This is the prerequisite that makes the migration safe, and it pays off whether or not that migration happens.

Scope:
- Pick a runner. Zero-dependency-to-minimal matters here; the repo currently has no package.json at all, so this bead is where one appears. node:test plus node:assert is the lowest-friction option given Node 26 is already installed and requires no new dependency at all; justify the choice over vitest/jest on the grounds that a browser prototype with no build step should not acquire a heavy test toolchain.
- Write the first test red before any implementation change. engine.js is the target: the pure rule registry and createEngine have no DOM dependency, so they are directly testable today, before any migration.
- Cover the semantics recorded in the memory number-up-eval-rule-semantics-current-candidate-numeric: numeric tiles replace and set pending, operator tiles apply to (currentNumber, pending), operator chains act as verbs, operators with no pending operand yield an invalid result. Also cover each failure rule boundary (DOWN, flat, invalid) since notUp.failed depends on the check order at engine.js:69-71.
- Add a typecheck/test script convention and wire both into the session-close quality gates described in AGENTS.md.
- Document the red-green loop in AGENTS.md so future sessions follow it without being asked.

Acceptance:
- At least one test written and observed failing before its implementation existed, with the failure recorded on the bead.
- npm test (or the chosen command) passes and is documented in AGENTS.md.
- Tests run from a clean checkout with a single documented command and no manual setup.

Notes: Deliberately scoped to engine.js. Do not attempt DOM coverage of main.js here — it has no DOM test harness and building one is a separate decision. Test the pure logic first; that is where the bugs that matter live.
acceptance_criteria: Test runner installed, first test written red-then-green against engine.js, documented command in AGENTS.md, wired into quality gates.
notes:
Runner: node:test + node:assert (Node v26.10.0, zero deps, no install). Justification: no-build-step browser prototype opening via file:// must not acquire heavy vitest/jest toolchain; stdlib runner runs from clean checkout with single command 'npm test' (node --test test/), no node_modules needed.

RED (observed before implementation change): mutated test to naive expectation 'operator with no pending leaves Number unchanged' (assert ev.valid==true, result==5 for attempt(5,'up','+')). npm/node --test failed as expected: 13 pass / 1 fail. Failing test: 'operators with no pending operand yield an invalid result' at test/engine.test.js:45 — AssertionError ERR_ASSERTION false !== true (actual:false expected:true, operator strictEqual). Confirms test is red-capable: engine correctly returns valid=false result=null for pending==null (engine.js:53).

GREEN: restored correct expectation (valid==false, result==null); no engine change needed — test-correctness fix only. engine.js eval/notUp semantics already match memory number-up-eval-rule-semantics-current-candidate-numeric. npm test now 14 pass / 0 fail. Coverage: numeric REPLACE+pending, operator apply (current,pending), verb chains (+ + +), no-pending invalid, floor passthrough, notUp order invalid/DOWN/flat (engine.js:69-71), end-to-end DOWN/flat/invalid fail + UP pass, createEngine wiring/fallback/history.

Files: test/engine.test.js (new), package.json (new, test script), AGENTS.md Build&Test (runner + red-green loop + quality gate). Verified: npm test green, no node_modules present (clean-checkout single command). No DOM coverage of main.js per scope.
close_reason: Red observed+recorded (1 fail on naive no-pending expectation), green 14/0 via test-correctness fix (no engine change), npm test documented in AGENTS.md, single-command clean checkout verified (no node_modules). Tree left dirty for coordinator.

title: Ideate: make the current Number the player mark, centrally
description:
The premise says **"the dot IS the current Number"** (_the_beginning.md:66).
The build says otherwise. `buildGrid` renders the player as a fixed circle
`r = 30` (src/play.ts:159) with the value inside it at `font-size: 30px`
(style.css:128) — a 60px disc holding a 30px numeral in a 100px cell. The
loudest number on the page is not on the board at all: it is `#number` at
`font-size: 26px` in the header (play.html:16, style.css:70), up the top,
away from the position. So the player's eye splits: one glance at the
position to know *where*, one glance up at the header to know *how much*. The
thing that is supposed to be a single object is rendered as two.

And rendering the value properly at the position runs out of room — which is
the actual constraint to design against, not an incidental annoyance. It is
already breaking today:

- 3 digits at 30px monospace ≈ 54px of ink inside a 60px disc: the chord is
  narrower than the text, so it spills past the circle.
- 4+ digits overflow the 100px cell entirely.
- `fmtNumber` returns the string `INVALID` for a non-finite Number
  (src/play.ts:170) — 7 characters at 30px in a 60px disc. Currently
  guaranteed-broken, not an edge case.
- This is not a rare state. Under `eval`, one run reaches it in four moves:
  touch 9 (pending 9), then `×` three times → 9, 81, 729, 6561. Under `add`
  on world a, 40+ is routine. Under `replace` (Becoming) you are small again
  next move.

So the room problem is structural: the player's own value is unbounded, the
cell is fixed. Any fix has to answer "what does a 4-digit you look like in a
1-cell space" without making the number unreadable, and without shrinking the
board.

## What to explore

This is an ideate-and-prototype bead. Several genuinely different means of
tying value to position, each with its own cost:

**A. The numeral is the mark — drop the disc.** The dot was a placeholder for
a character that does not exist. Delete it and let a bare, differently-treated
numeral *be* the player. Maximum literalness, zero size problem for 1–2
digits, and it makes the "you become what you touch" reading of `replace`
stronger. Risk: a free-floating numeral reads as a tile. Needs the player's
type treatment to differ from tiles by more than colour (weight, size, outline,
and the up/down flash).

**B. The mark scales with magnitude.** `r = f(digitCount)` or `f(log value)`,
with the font scaling with the radius. "You get bigger as you get bigger."
The strongest expression of the premise, and it turns the room problem into
the point: a 4-digit you is a big you filling its cell. Peripheral legibility
too — magnitude is readable without reading digits. Risk: with `×` chains the
radius explodes across four orders of magnitude in three moves, so continuous
proportional scaling will not work; discrete digit-count bands will.
Consistent with the hexagon experiment (num-1st) shrinking cells further.

**C. Fixed disc, arc as the meter.** Keep the disc a constant size and encode
magnitude in a surrounding arc or ring. Separates legibility (constant glyph)
from magnitude (variable surround). Costs a second channel to decode, and the
arc has to be learned.

**D. Digits stacked or compressed.** Vertical stacking for 4+ digits, or `1k` /
`1M` abbreviation. Stacking is exact and ugly. Abbreviation loses the value,
and the value is the entire subject of the game — treat this as the option to
reject, and record why.

**E. A trailing wake.** The previous values follow you at decreasing size and
opacity, current at the head. Makes superposition history visible *in place*,
replacing the transient delta glyph with a body. Highest ceiling: the board
itself becomes the history. Highest cost: clutter, and it competes with the
fly/delta FX in `animateSuperpose`.

**F. One readout, not two.** The cheapest move, and a precondition for the
others: `#number` in the header is currently a first-class readout that the
player will keep using. If the board mark becomes authoritative, the header
stat should go, or be demoted to debug-only. Otherwise you have added a second
place to look and made the split worse.

## The paired half

If the Number moves to the board, the up/down/flat signal has to move with it.
`flashStatus` (src/play.ts:181) colours the *header* number green/red/grey
for 450ms. That is the outcome signal — the game's only feedback about whether
UP happened — and it currently fires somewhere the player is not looking.
Nothing in the board encodes up/down at all. Any version of this that adds a
prominent number but leaves the flash in the header has moved half the problem
and made the header harder to drop.

Same ground as num-bpq (quiet normal play): the board doing this work is what
lets the text narration go away.

## How to tell whether it worked

Write the hypothesis down *before* building, in the form the notebooks use
(variants/<id>.md, hypothesis + what would disprove it). The observable is
attention, not preference:

- can a player state their current Number after ~20 moves without looking at
  the top of the screen
- do they stop glancing up between moves
- when asked "what are you?", do they point at the board or at the header

Do not accept a version that merely looks better in a screenshot. The failure
mode to watch for: a mark that is beautiful and legible at 2 digits and
useless at 5, which means the fix only works in easy worlds.

## Where

- `src/play.ts` — `buildGrid` (src/play.ts:158) builds the player node,
  `fmtNumber` (src/play.ts:170), `flashStatus` (src/play.ts:181),
  `render` (src/play.ts:321), `animateSuperpose` (src/play.ts:195) for FX
  collisions, `renderStatus` (src/play.ts:273)
- `play.html` — `#number` header stat (play.html:16), `#grid` viewBox
- `style.css` — `.dot` (style.css:120), `#player .pnum` (style.css:128),
  `pop` keyframes (style.css:151), `.fly`/`.delta` (style.css:157)
- `src/engine.ts` — should not change; Number is already unbounded there
- `_the_beginning.md` — the dot-is-the-Number claim is the thing under test
- README.md — if the header readout is demoted or removed, the page-parity
  notes there need to follow

## Constraints

- No new persistent primitive. This is a representation change, not a mechanic.
  No digit counter, no "size" stat, nothing that outlives `R`.
- Movement, keys, swipe, and the FX must keep working; the mark must not cover
  adjacent tiles it is meant to invite you into.
- Touch play first: the board is `min(560px, 94vw)`, so on a phone a cell is
  ~75px of real estate and a 5-digit numeral is a genuine squeeze.
- Pure fit maths (radius/font as a function of digit count, the chord-vs-text-
  width constraint) belongs in a `node:test`-covered function; only the SVG
  emission stays DOM.
- Prototype constraints hold: strict TypeScript, no runtime dependency, `dist/`
  committed, page opens from `file://`.
design:
Start with the fit maths, because it decides which visual options survive.

For n digits at font-size fs in a monospace face, advance width ≈ `0.6 · fs`,
so the text is `w = 0.6 · n · fs` wide and about `0.7 · fs` tall. To sit inside
a disc of radius r the widest chord available at the text's vertical extent is
`2 · sqrt(r² − (0.35·fs)²)`. Feasibility is then

    0.6 · n · fs  ≤  2 · sqrt(r² − (0.35·fs)²)

so the largest fs that fits a given (n, r) is solvable in closed form (or by a
few bisection steps — either is fine, it is a pure function and belongs in
`src/` with `node:test` coverage). Feed it `n = fmtNumber(state.number).length`,
which already handles `INVALID`.

Two caveats to encode rather than assume:

- `0.6` is an approximation of the advance ratio. Calibrate it once at runtime
  with `getComputedTextLength()` on a real numeral and pass the measured ratio
  into the pure function as a parameter. Do not hardcode a guess.
- The cap must come from the cell, not the disc: `r ≤ 0.5 · CELL · fill` with
  `fill ≈ 0.9`, so a marked player never invades a neighbour's cell.

Recommended sequence, cheapest to most committed:

1. **F alone**, as a measurement baseline. Demote `#number` to debug-only and
   play it. If players still track their value fine, the rest is optional. This
   is a few lines and it tells you whether the problem is real to players.
2. **A + B together**: bare numeral as the mark, radius and font stepped by
   digit-count bands (1–2 / 3 / 4+), with the up/down/flat colour moved onto the
   board mark. Covers the literalism and the scalability, and reuses the existing
   `pop` animation by scaling it from the band radius.
3. **E** only if 1 and 2 land and the delta glyph still reads as transient — the
   wake is the strongest idea but it multiplies against `animateSuperpose`, which
   already flies a tile into the destination cell and raises a delta glyph off
   it. The player lands where the FX are; that collision is the whole cost.

Radius bands, for calibration against a 100px cell: 1–2 digits r≈34,
3 digits r≈42, 4+ digits r≈47. Beyond that the mark is a neighbour tile with a
number in it, and abbreviation is the honest fallback even though it loses
fidelity — log it as a known compromise rather than pretending it is clean.

Relates to num-1st: hex cells are ~13–25% smaller at equal board width, so any
radius cap chosen here must survive the hex case, or the two beads will
contradict each other when they land.

- [ ] Chosen mark is legible at 1, 2, 3, and 5+ digits, and at `INVALID`
- [ ] Mark stays inside its own cell; adjacent tiles remain fully readable
- [ ] Up/down/flat signal lives where the Number lives, not only in the header
- [ ] Digit-fit maths (radius/font vs digit count) is pure and `node:test` covered; the 0.6 advance ratio is measured, not assumed
- [ ] Touch-width layout checked at ~75px per cell
- [ ] `npm run verify` green and rebuilt `dist/` committed

title: Experiment: hexagonal lattice layout
description:
Experiment: what does the game feel like on a hexagonal lattice instead of the
5×5 square grid?

The square grid is currently load-bearing in a way the engine never sees.
`Pos` is `{x, y}` (src/play.ts:5) and `WORLDS` is a literal 5×5 `rows` array
with `.` as the start hole (src/world.ts:10); movement is a hardcoded
4-entry `DIRECTIONS` table with unit steps (src/play.ts:328); the boundary test
in `tryMove` is a rectangle check (src/play.ts:349); `cellCenter` and
`buildGrid` place `CELL = 100` squares in a 500×500 viewBox (src/play.ts:72,
src/play.ts:121); keyboard maps 4 arrows/WASD/numpad to 4 directions
(src/play.ts:432); swipe resolves to the dominant axis of 4
(src/play.ts:527). None of that is in `src/engine.ts`, which is already
layout-free — good — but the layout is welded to the page.

## The question worth asking

Not "can we draw hexagons". The question is whether a 6-neighbour lattice makes
superposition *more* legible or *less*.

- More choice per tile: three ways onward instead of two, so planning a chain of
  operators is a wider search. Good for Verbs.
- Worse direction legibility: 4 arrow keys cannot cleanly express 6 neighbours.
  Diagonal intent has to be approximated (last-pressed axis, or 2 nearest
  hexes) and an approximation the player cannot feel will read as the game
  ignoring them. This is the risk.

## Scope of the experiment

- Abstract the lattice behind a small interface so square and hex are
  swappable: a cell list, a centre per cell, and six (or four) neighbours per
  cell plus a step. Candidate: `src/lattice.ts` exporting `SquareLattice` and
  `HexLattice` (pointy-top and flat-top are worth one variable each; flat-top
  with horizontal rows keeps `rows` intact if rows-as-world-data survives, which
  is the cheap first cut).
- Express movement as a lattice step, not `dx/dy`. The engine still sees
  `attempt(number, directionLabel, tile)`; direction labels for hex need honest
  names (the six compass directions) since the debug notebook will print them.
- Pick the input scheme deliberately and record it: 4 keys approximated, 6
  keys (QEZ/numrow?), or nearest-hex-of-swipe-vector by angle. Whichever, the
  mapping must be visible (num-bpq's notebook panel) rather than guessed.
- Hex worlds need a hex-shaped `WORLDS` entry and `generateWorld` needs to fill
  a hex region, including the boundary shape (hex grids are awkward to bound —
  a rectangle in axial coords leaves ragged edges).
- Fit the viewBox: 5×5 hexes need a smaller cell size or a wider/taller canvas;
  the play page currently hardcodes a square world. Touch play matters here —
  this is a swipe game on phones.
- Superposition animation must still read: the flying tile lands *into* a hex,
  the dot's Number pops, the delta glyph rises off the hex centre.

## Constraints

- Square grid stays the default and stays in the gallery. This is an experiment
  in `?layout=hex` style, not a replacement, until the hypothesis has evidence.
- Prototype constraint holds: no build-time dependency, sources stay strict
  TypeScript, `dist/` still committed, page still opens from `file://`.
- No new persistent primitive. Geometry is not a mechanic.
- Pure lattice math (centres, neighbour indices, step, bounds) goes in
  `src/lattice.ts` with `node:test` coverage — this is the one part of the page
  that can be tested without a DOM, and neighbour tables are exactly where off-
  by-one bugs hide.
- Per the AGENTS.md convention: if this graduates to a named layout, it gets a
  notebook file (`layouts/hex.md` or a `variants/` entry) with the hypothesis
  and dated feedback, and the gallery renders it.

## Where

- `src/world.ts` — hex-shaped worlds, `generateWorld` over a hex region,
  `findStart`
- `src/play.ts` — `Pos`, `DIRECTIONS`, `tryMove` boundary + step, `cellCenter`,
  `buildGrid`, `KEYS`, swipe angle resolution, `CELL`/viewBox
- `play.html` — svg viewBox, help row key legend
- `style.css` — hex cell fills, the dot, tile text centering
- `src/engine.ts` — should not change; if it has to, that is a finding
- README.md — debug/param docs alongside the existing `?world=`/`?rule=` list

## Acceptance

- [ ] `?layout=hex` plays a full run on a hex lattice, start to failure
- [ ] Square grid is unchanged and still the default; gallery untouched
- [ ] Neighbour tables, centres, and step have `node:test` coverage
- [ ] The input mapping for 6 neighbours is explicit and documented in the
      notebook panel, not approximated silently
- [ ] Hypothesis recorded before implementation, feedback dated after playing
- [ ] `npm run verify` green and rebuilt `dist/` committed
design:
Cheapest honest first cut: flat-top hexes in offset rows.

Offset ("odd-r") coordinates keep `World.rows` exactly as it is today — a row
array per row, `.` still the start hole — so hex worlds are data-compatible
with square worlds and only the lattice geometry changes. Pointy-top needs
real axial/cube conversion; flat-top odd-r only needs
`centre(x, y) = { cx: 1.5 * R * x + (y & 1 ? 0.75 * R : 0), cy: sqrt(3) * R * y }`
and a six-entry neighbour table with x-offsets that depend on row parity.

Suggested seam in `src/lattice.ts`:

    export interface Lattice {
      readonly cols: number; readonly rows: number;
      centre(x: number, y: number): { cx: number; cy: number };
      step(x: number, y: number, dir: Direction): Pos | null; // null = edge
      directions: readonly Direction[];                       // square: 4, hex: 6
      nearest(x: number, y: number, vx: number, vy: number): Direction; // swipe
      cellShape(cx: number, cy: number): SVGElement;          // or path data
    }

`nearest` is the honest place for swipe: pick the direction whose centre
maximises the dot product with the swipe vector, instead of today's
dominant-axis threshold. That removes the diagonal lie entirely and is unit
testable.

Keyboard is the hard part. Do not silently map 4 keys onto 6 directions.
Options to try, in order of honesty: six keys with the two diagonals on Q/E/Z/C
or the numpad corners (Numpad7/9/1/3), keep WASD for the four cardinals and
document the diagonals as optional. Whatever ships, the help row and the debug
notebook must print the actual mapping.

viewBox: keep one canvas and let the lattice report its own bounds
(`lattice.viewBox`) so a 5-wide hex board and a 5×5 square board both fill the
space. `CELL = 100` stops being a constant and becomes a derived size.

World data: add a hex world to `WORLDS` (same `rows` shape) plus a
`generateHexWorld(seed)` — or parameterise `generateWorld` by lattice and keep
one seeded generator, which is better because it keeps the seeded-world story
identical between layouts. Boundary: rows are 5 long in odd-r, so the ragged
edge is two half-hexes at alternating row ends; decide whether to keep the
rectangle (ugly corners, trivial data) or trim to a clean hex-shaped board
(cleaner board, generator needs a fill predicate).
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `?layout=hex` plays a full run on a hex lattice, start to failure
- [ ] Square grid unchanged and still the default; gallery untouched
- [ ] Neighbour tables, centres, and step have `node:test` coverage
- [ ] The input mapping for 6 neighbours is explicit and documented in the notebook panel, not approximated silently
- [ ] Hypothesis recorded before implementation, feedback dated after playing
- [ ] `npm run verify` green and rebuilt `dist/` committed

title: Make /debug the lab notebook; keep normal play quiet
description:
Debug mode becomes the laboratory notebook. Normal mode stops narrating and lets
the world and the superposition animation carry the meaning.

Today the verbose text IS normal mode: `showObservation` in src/play.ts:244
rewrites the whole arithmetic of every move into `#observation` ("You moved
UP / SUPERPOSITION / 0 + 9 / Result: 9 / Number went UP: YES (Δ +9)") — while
the same fact is already drawn on the board by `animateSuperpose`
(src/play.ts:195): the tile flies from the player into the destination cell,
the dot's Number pops to the new value, a `↑ +9` delta glyph rises off the tile,
and the header Number flashes up/down/flat. So normal play says the same thing
twice, in text, forever.

Meanwhile `/debug` only reveals four header stats and a 8-row tail of the move
history (src/play.ts:309). That is not a notebook.

## Debug mode (verbose) — target

Debug is where a designer reads the machine. When it is on:

- the existing verbose observation copy, always, including blocked moves and
  run-over details
- pending operand and which tile set it (the `ctx.pending` the engine keeps
  internally and currently never surfaces)
- collision rule name, failure rule name, world key + name, variant or
  `rule × fail` custom pairing, generation seed, and the current URL params
- full move log for the run, not a tail: turn, from-position, direction,
  destination tile, oldNumber, pending at entry, result, delta, wentUp, failed
  + failReason
- run totals: turns survived, peak Number, final Number, counts of up/down/flat
  and invalid moves
- copy-to-clipboard of the whole dump, so a run can be pasted into a
  variants/<id>.md notebook or a bug report without retyping (the mailto
  feedback path at src/play.ts:286 already does a lesser version of this)

## Normal mode (quiet) — target

- the per-move arithmetic block is gone from `#observation`
- state still has to be legible, so: the destination cell shows the result for
  a beat after the collision (short-lived `= 9` beside the popped Number), and
  blocked moves get one short line ("Blocked — edge of world"), run-over gets
  the run-over block
- the help/URL chrome stays, but nothing numeric that the board already shows

## Constraints

- No new persistent primitives. Debug readouts are instrumentation over state
  that already exists (Number, position, Up, superposition), not a score or
  HP. Do not add a "high score" or a stat that survives a restart.
- The prototype constraint holds: bundle still opens from `file://`, `dist/`
  still committed, sources still strict TypeScript.
- Debug state is not currently in the URL, so a debug run cannot be shared or
  reloaded — decide whether `debug=1` should round-trip through `syncUrl`.
- Anything pure enough to test goes in `src/engine.ts` with `node:test`
  coverage; the debug panel render itself is DOM and has no harness, so keep
  the aggregation logic (run totals, log formatting) in a pure function that
  can be tested.

## Where

- `src/play.ts` — `showObservation`, `showBlocked`, `showRunOver`,
  `renderHistory`, `renderStatus`, `toggleDebug`, `feedbackHref`, `syncUrl`
- `src/engine.ts` — surface `pending` at attempt entry on `MoveEvent` so the
  notebook can show it
- `play.html` — the `debug-only` panels, header stats, help row
- `style.css` — `body.debug` / `.debug-only` at style.css:266
- `README.md` — the `/` and `?debug=1` lines, plus the "run state attached to
  feedback" claim at README.md:83
design:
Split the copy in src/play.ts into a verbose layer and a quiet layer rather
than adding a second code path.

- Extract the per-move verbose block into `verboseObservation(ev)` — pure-ish,
  returns a DocumentFragment or an array of {class, text} — and let
  `showObservation` pick `verboseObservation(ev)` when `state.debug`, else a
  one-line quiet summary.
- Add a pure `summariseRun(history: MoveEvent[]): RunTotals` and
  `formatMoveLog(history: MoveEvent[]): string[]` in src/engine.ts (or a new
  src/debug.ts importing from engine) so they are unit-testable without a DOM.
  `formatMoveLog` replaces `renderHistory` and is reused by copy-to-clipboard.
- To log pending operand, extend `AttemptBase` with `pendingAtEntry: number |
  null` and set it in `createEngine.attempt` from the `pending` variable before
  `ctx` is handed to the rule. That is the only engine change and it is
  observable-only.
- Copy-to-clipboard: `navigator.clipboard.writeText` wrapped in try/catch with a
  textarea fallback, since the page also runs over `file://`.
- Result-on-cell: reuse `fxLayer` in `animateSuperpose` and append a short-lived
  `= N` text node at the destination cell; no new persistent state.
- Keep `debug` out of `syncUrl` unless the round-trip is decided; if it is,
  `?debug=1` deep links already forward through src/gallery.ts:18.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Normal play shows no per-move arithmetic text; the board and animation
      alone convey Number, direction, and outcome
- [ ] `/debug` (and `?debug=1`) shows verbose observation plus pending operand,
      rule/fail/world/variant/seed, full move log, run totals, and a
      copy-to-clipboard dump
- [ ] Run totals and move-log formatting are covered by `node:test`
- [ ] No new persistent primitive; nothing survives `R` except run-scoped data
- [ ] `npm run verify` green and rebuilt `dist/` committed
- [ ] README `/` and `?debug=1` lines updated to describe the notebook

title: Apply best-practice TypeScript to the work completed so far
description:
Retrofit the existing code to the TypeScript setup established in the parent bead, migrating behind the safety net the TDD bead provides.

- Convert engine.js, world.js, main.js, gallery.js, variants.js from IIFE globals to ES modules, keeping the existing file boundaries.
- Run strict tsc across all of it and triage every diagnostic into: real bug, missing annotation, or intentional dynamic behaviour.

title: Input robustness: CapsLock kills WASD; C/F silently wipe runs (review finding 5)
description: Verified at HEAD: MOVE_KEYS maps only lowercase w/a/s/d (+ hex q/e/z/c) plus numpad codes; with CapsLock on, e.key='W' and e.code='KeyW' are both unmapped, so movement silently dies (play.ts:566-624). Fix: normalize e.key to lowercase for move lookup. In square mode C (cycle rule) and F (cycle fail) sit adjacent to WASD and both restart the run with no confirmation — one fat finger wipes a run mid-flight. Hex mode already demonstrates remapping is acceptable (C became the SE move; rule-cycle moved to V). Options: move rule/fail cycling behind a modifier or to distant keys, mirror the hex C->V remap, or confirm before wiping a run that has history.
